o: A[i][j][k] = i·(j OR k) for 0 ≤ i,j,k < n; find the largest n whose total sum ≤ s (s up to 10^15). Factor the sum: Σ_i i = n(n−1)/2 and T(n) = Σ_{j,k<n} (j|k), so S(n) = n(n−1)/2 · T(n). T(n) decomposes by bit: for each bit b, with A_b = count of numbers below n having bit b, the number of pairs where bit b appears in the OR is 2·A_b·(n−A_b) + A_b². S(n) is monotone in n, so binary search works; alternatively grow n incrementally maintaining T with bit counters.
k: S(n) factors as (Σi)·(Σ_{j,k} j|k) = n(n−1)/2 · T(n) because the i-dimension separates.
T(n) = Σ_bits (2·A_b·n − A_b²), where A_b (count of values < n with bit b) has a closed form from binary digits.
S(n) is strictly increasing for n ≥ 2, enabling binary search; answers stay below ~10^4 so 64-bit arithmetic is safe.

a.n: Approach 1: Incremental growth with bit counters
a.i: Insert values v = 1, 2, 3, … into the OR-sum. Adding value v to a current set of size v contributes 2·(v·v + Σ_{bits b not in v} cnt_b) + v to T: each existing partner contributes v plus the partner's exclusive bits, counted once per ordered side, plus the (v,v) pair.
s: Maintain cnt[b] = how many inserted values have bit b, and running T
For v = 1,2,…: add 2·(v² + Σ_{b∉v} cnt[b]) + v to T, then update cnt
After each insertion compute S = C(n,2)·T; stop when S > s and return n−1
a.t: O(answer · 40) ≈ O(6·10^5) — one pass over bits per inserted value

a.i: A_b(n) = ⌊n/2^{b+1}⌋·2^b + max(0, n mod 2^{b+1} − 2^b) counts values below n with bit b set. Then T(n) = Σ_b (2·A_b·n − A_b²) and S(n) = n(n−1)/2·T(n); binary search the largest n with S(n) ≤ s.
s: Implement ok(n) computing S(n) via the per-bit formula
Binary search n in [1, 20000] for the largest n with ok(n)
a.t: O(20 · log(20000)) — constant-bit evaluation inside a binary search

w: The factorization Σ_i·Σ_{j,k} is the whole problem — without it you'd face an O(n³) sum. Verify with s=10: S(2)=1·3=3 ≤ 10, S(3)=3·15=45 > 10 → answer 2. Beware overflow near the boundary in fixed-width languages (use __int128/double guards). Edge case s=0 → answer 1 since S(1)=0. Follow-up: generalize to A[i][j][k]=i·(j AND k) — same decomposition, different pair-count formula.
